lessons.title: The Federal Reserve
lessons.mainIdea: The Federal Reserve steers the economy by moving interest rates, trying to keep both inflation and unemployment low, and it is built to act faster than Congress and with less political pressure.
reading: In 1907 a panic swept through New York banks. Depositors lined up to pull out their money, healthy banks failed because they could not get cash fast enough, and a single private banker, J. P. Morgan, gathered rich men in his library to organize a rescue. Congress decided the country should not depend on one man again. In 1913 it created the *Federal Reserve*, the nation's central bank, with a board in Washington and twelve regional banks, one of them on LaSalle Street in Chicago. Its first job was to be a lender of last resort: a bank that lends to banks when everyone else is afraid to.

Today the Fed's main tool is the *interest rate*, the price of borrowing money. A committee of Fed officials meets about eight times a year and sets a target for the rate banks charge each other overnight. Every other rate follows it: mortgages, car loans, credit cards, business loans. Raising the rate makes borrowing dearer, so households and firms spend less, which cools prices. Cutting it does the opposite. This is *monetary policy*. In 2020 the Fed cut its rate to nearly zero to keep the pandemic economy alive. Between March 2022 and July 2023 it raised the rate from near zero to over five percent, the fastest climb in forty years, to fight the inflation that followed.

Congress gave the Fed two goals, often called the *dual mandate*: maximum employment and stable prices. The two conflict at the worst moments. Raising rates to cut inflation also slows hiring; in 1982 the Fed's war on inflation pushed unemployment above ten percent. Cutting rates to create jobs risks inflation. Fed officials describe their work as trying to slow a car on ice, since a rate change takes a year or more to show its full effect and they cannot see the road ahead. The 2022 to 2023 case turned out better than most feared: inflation fell sharply and unemployment stayed near four percent, though economists still argue how much credit the Fed deserves.

The Fed is deliberately insulated from politics. Its governors serve fourteen-year terms, its chair is appointed by the president and confirmed by the Senate for four years, and it funds itself rather than depending on Congress for a budget. Supporters say this is essential, because a president facing an election will always want lower rates now and inflation later. Critics from both parties say an unelected body with that much power over jobs and mortgages should answer more directly to voters. Presidents have complained about the Fed publicly and privately for a century. The design, so far, has held.

words.d: the central bank of the United States, created in 1913, which sets interest rates and lends to banks in a crisis
the price of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage of the amount borrowed per year
the Federal Reserve's use of interest rates and the money supply to steer the economy
the Fed's two goals set by Congress: maximum employment and stable prices

look.title: What Congress Told the Fed to Do
look.text: The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and the Federal Open Market Committee shall maintain long run growth of the monetary and credit aggregates commensurate with the economy's long run potential to increase production, so as to promote effectively the goals of maximum employment, stable prices, and moderate long-term interest rates.
look.cite: Federal Reserve Act, Section 2A, as amended by Congress in 1977
look.prompt: The law names three goals, not two, and gives no numbers for any of them. Who decides what stable prices means, and why might Congress have chosen to leave that open?

check.q: What was the main reason Congress created the Federal Reserve in 1913?
choices: To collect income taxes
To set the federal budget
To print paper money for the first time
To act as a lender of last resort after the Panic of 1907
check.why: The 1907 panic showed the country needed a central bank that could lend to banks when private lenders would not.

check.q: The Fed raises its interest rate target sharply. What is the intended effect?
choices: Borrowing becomes more expensive, spending slows and inflation cools
Borrowing becomes cheaper and hiring speeds up
Taxes rise and the deficit falls
Imports become cheaper
check.why: Higher rates raise the cost of loans, which slows spending across the economy and reduces price pressure.

check.q: Why do Fed governors serve fourteen-year terms and why does the Fed fund itself?
choices: To keep the Fed under close control of Congress
To shield the Fed's rate decisions from short-term political pressure
To let the president set rates directly
To reduce the national debt
check.why: The long terms and independent funding are designed so the Fed can raise rates when needed even if elected officials object.

lessons.title: Trade and Tariffs
lessons.mainIdea: Trade lets countries specialize in what they do best and makes goods cheaper, but it also moves jobs, and tariffs protect some workers at a cost to others.
reading: Illinois is one of the two largest soybean-growing states in the country, and for years its biggest customer was China. A farmer near Decatur sells beans that ride a barge down the Illinois River to the Gulf and cross the Pacific in a bulk ship. In return, the container ships that dock on the West Coast carry phones, clothes and machine parts to Chicago's rail yards. An *export* is something sold to another country; an *import* is something bought from one. The United States imports more than it exports, and the gap is the *trade deficit*.

Why trade at all? Because a country, like a person, gains by doing what it does relatively best and buying the rest. Illinois soil and machinery grow soybeans cheaper than almost anywhere. Factories in Vietnam sew shirts cheaper than any American factory could. When each side specializes and trades, both end up with more beans and more shirts than if each tried to make everything. Economists call this *comparative advantage*, and it is one of the few ideas nearly all of them accept. The catch is that gains are spread thin across millions of shoppers while the losses land hard on particular towns.

Those losses are real. When cheaper imports arrived, steel mills in Gary and Granite City, auto-parts plants in Rockford and furniture makers across the Midwest shed jobs, and many of the workers never found pay as good again. A *tariff* is a tax on imports, and its purpose is to raise the price of the foreign product so the domestic one can compete. In 2018 the federal government put a twenty-five percent tariff on imported steel, and a mill in Granite City, Illinois, restarted furnaces it had shut down. Steelworkers there saw the tariff as rescue.

Then China answered with tariffs of its own on American soybeans. Illinois farmers lost their best market almost overnight, and the federal government paid farmers tens of billions of dollars to cover the losses. Meanwhile every American factory that uses steel, from carmakers to can makers, paid more for it. That is the standard pattern: a tariff helps the protected industry, hurts the industries that buy its product, invites retaliation against exporters, and raises prices for shoppers. Whether it is worth it depends on how much you value a steel town's jobs against everyone else's costs. That is a political judgment, and economics can only tell you the size of each side.

words.d: a good or service sold to buyers in another country
a good or service bought from sellers in another country
the amount by which a country's imports exceed its exports
the gain that comes when each country specializes in what it produces relatively best and trades for the rest
a tax on imported goods, which raises their price to protect domestic producers

look.title: Granite City and Decatur
look.text: In 2018 a steelworker in Granite City goes back to a job that pays well because a tariff made imported steel dearer. Three hours north, a soybean farmer near Decatur watches her biggest buyer, China, stop ordering in reply to that same tariff. In Chicago, a company that makes steel cans pays more for every sheet it buys and raises its prices. All three are Illinois residents. All three vote.
look.prompt: List who gained and who lost from the 2018 steel tariff, in Illinois alone. If you were a senator from Illinois, what evidence would you want before deciding how to vote on renewing it?

check.q: What is a tariff?
choices: A limit on the number of goods exported
A tax on imported goods
A subsidy paid to farmers
A rule setting the price of steel
check.why: A tariff taxes imports to raise their price so domestic producers can compete.

check.q: Which group in Illinois was hurt when China retaliated against U.S. steel tariffs in 2018?
choices: Steelworkers in Granite City
Soybean farmers who exported to China
Chicago consumers of Chinese phones
Federal Reserve officials
check.why: China put tariffs on American soybeans, and Illinois farmers lost their largest export market.

check.q: What does comparative advantage say about trade?
choices: A country should make everything it can at home
Trade always creates jobs in every town
Both sides gain when each specializes in what it produces relatively best
Imports are always harmful
check.why: Specialization and trade leave both countries with more total goods, even though particular industries lose.

lessons.title: Budgets, Saving and Credit
lessons.mainIdea: A budget is a plan for scarce dollars, compound interest makes saved money grow and borrowed money grow against you, and a credit score records how you have handled both.
reading: A first paycheck is an economics lesson in miniature. A student working twenty hours a week at fifteen dollars an hour in Illinois earns about three hundred dollars, and after taxes are withheld the deposit is smaller. Then the wants line up: a phone bill, gas, food with friends, a pair of shoes, a savings goal. A *budget* is a written plan for where the money goes before it goes there. One common rule divides take-home pay into roughly half for needs, thirty percent for wants and twenty percent for saving and paying down debt. The exact numbers matter less than the act of deciding in advance, because money that is not assigned tends to leave.

Saving works because of *interest*, the price of using money over time. When you save, a bank pays you interest; when you borrow, you pay it. The power comes from compounding. *Compound interest* means each year's interest is added to the balance, so the next year's interest is figured on a larger amount. One thousand dollars growing at seven percent a year becomes about two thousand in ten years, four thousand in twenty, and nearly fifteen thousand in forty. The early years look slow and the late years look like magic, which is why the most valuable thing a young saver has is time.

Compounding runs the other way on debt. A credit card charges interest by the year, stated as the *APR*, the annual percentage rate, and card rates often run above twenty percent. A one-thousand-dollar balance paid down only by the minimum each month can take years to clear and cost hundreds in interest, while the same thousand dollars saved would have been earning for you. A card is a tool: paid in full every month, it costs nothing and builds a record. Carried, it is one of the most expensive loans an ordinary person can take. The difference is entirely in the habit.

That record becomes a *credit score*, a number, usually between three hundred and eight hundred fifty, that lenders use to predict whether you will repay. It rises when you pay on time and keep balances low relative to your limits, and it falls when you miss payments or max out cards. The score follows you to the landlord, the car dealer, sometimes the employer, and it sets the interest rate you will pay for a car or a house. Two people buying the same car can pay thousands of dollars apart over the loan because of it. Illinois requires every high school student to take a consumer education course for exactly this reason: the rules are simple, the cost of not knowing them is not.

words.d: a plan for how income will be spent, saved and used to pay debts
the price paid for using money over time, earned on savings and charged on loans
interest figured on both the original amount and the interest already added to it
annual percentage rate, the yearly cost of a loan or credit card stated as a percentage
a number lenders use to predict how likely a person is to repay, based on their payment history

look.title: One Thousand Dollars, Left Alone
look.unit: dollars at seven percent a year, rounded
look.cite: compound-interest arithmetic; seven percent is close to the long-run average return of a broad stock index, before inflation
look.prompt: The first decade adds about a thousand dollars and the last adds more than seven thousand. Why? What does this table say about a dollar saved at eighteen versus one saved at forty?

check.q: What is compound interest?
choices: Interest charged only on the original loan amount
A fee for opening a bank account
Interest figured on the original amount plus the interest already added
The interest rate set by the Federal Reserve
check.why: Compounding means interest earns interest, which is why growth speeds up over time.

check.q: Why can a credit card be both free and very expensive?
choices: Paid in full each month it costs nothing; carried, its high APR compounds against you
It is free for students and expensive for adults
Cards are free in Illinois and taxed elsewhere
The APR is charged only on the first purchase
check.why: Card interest applies only to balances carried past the due date, and rates above twenty percent make carried balances costly.

check.q: Which action would most likely raise a credit score over time?
choices: Maxing out several cards
Paying every bill on time and keeping balances low
Never using credit at all
Opening many new cards at once
check.why: Scores reward a record of on-time payments and low balances relative to credit limits.

lessons.title: Investing, Insurance and College
lessons.mainIdea: Investing trades risk for growth, insurance trades a small certain cost for protection against a large uncertain one, and college is the biggest investment most students will make.
reading: Saving keeps money safe; investing puts it to work. A stock is a share of ownership in a company, and a bond is a loan to a company or government that pays interest. Stocks have grown faster over any long stretch of American history, but they swing: the market fell by about half in 2008 and 2009 before recovering. Bonds pay less and swing less. The core rule is *diversification*: spreading money across many investments so that no single failure ruins you. An *index fund* does this automatically by holding small pieces of hundreds of companies at very low cost, and for most people it beats trying to pick winners. A retirement account such as a 401(k) at work or an IRA adds tax advantages, and an employer match is free money.

Insurance solves a different problem. A car crash, a house fire or a serious illness could cost more than most families could ever save. Insurance pools that risk. Thousands of people each pay a *premium*, a regular payment, into a pool, and the pool pays the few who suffer a loss. The *deductible* is the amount you pay yourself before the insurance pays. A higher deductible means a lower premium, a sensible trade for someone with savings and a bad one for someone with none. Illinois requires drivers to carry liability insurance, and a hospital bill without health insurance is the most common way an American family falls into debt it cannot repay.

College is where all of these ideas meet. It is an investment: workers with a bachelor's degree earn, on average, well over half again as much as workers with only a high school diploma, and are far less likely to be unemployed. It also has a price. In 2024 a year of tuition and fees at a public four-year university averaged about eleven thousand dollars for in-state students and a private one about forty-three thousand, before housing and food. The sticker price is not what most students pay. The *net price*, what a family actually pays after grants and scholarships, is often far lower, and the only way to learn it is to apply.

The application that unlocks aid is the *FAFSA*, the free federal form every college uses to award grants, work-study and federal loans. The Pell Grant, which does not have to be repaid, pays lower-income students up to about seven thousand four hundred dollars a year. Illinois adds its own grant for state residents. The typical borrower who finishes a bachelor's degree owes roughly thirty thousand dollars, a burden that is manageable for a nurse or engineer and heavy for someone who left without a degree. That is the real risk: debt without the diploma. Two years at an Illinois community college and a transfer, a degree with a clear path to work, and a budget that starts before the first tuition bill are the diversification, insurance and compounding of this chapter, applied to your own life.

words.d: spreading money across many different investments so no single loss can ruin you
a low-cost investment that holds small pieces of hundreds of companies at once
the regular payment made to keep an insurance policy in force
the amount an insured person pays toward a loss before the insurance company pays
what a family actually pays for college after grants and scholarships are subtracted from the sticker price
the free federal application that colleges use to award grants, work-study and federal student loans

look.title: Two Letters in April
look.text: A senior in Joliet gets two admission letters. A private university lists tuition at forty-five thousand dollars but offers a grant that cuts her cost to eighteen thousand a year. A public university lists fourteen thousand and offers no grant. Her family can pay eight thousand a year. Both schools have her major. A cousin says the private school is obviously the better deal because the grant is so big.
look.prompt: Which school has the lower net price, and how much would she need to borrow at each over four years? What questions about her major and future pay should come before the money question?

check.q: Why do most financial advisers recommend an index fund for ordinary investors?
choices: It guarantees a fixed return every year
It is insured by the federal government
It avoids the stock market entirely
It spreads money across hundreds of companies at low cost
check.why: An index fund provides diversification cheaply, which reduces the risk of any single company's failure.

check.q: How does insurance make a large, rare loss affordable?
choices: The government pays every claim
Many people pay premiums into a pool that pays the few who suffer a loss
Each person saves enough to cover the loss
The deductible covers the whole cost
check.why: Insurance pools risk across thousands of payers, so no one has to save the full cost of a disaster alone.

check.q: What is the difference between a college's sticker price and its net price?
choices: Net price is what a family pays after grants and scholarships; sticker price is the listed cost
Sticker price includes housing; net price does not
Net price applies only to private colleges
They are the same for most students
check.why: Grants and scholarships often cut the listed price sharply, so the net price is the number that matters.

review.q: A city council spends its last two million dollars on a new fire truck instead of resurfacing a road. In economic terms, the road is the fire truck's what?
choices: Externality
Public good
Opportunity cost
Deficit
review.why: The next-best use given up, the road, is the opportunity cost of the truck.

review.q: Which event would most likely shift the supply of eggs and raise the price?
choices: A disease that kills millions of hens
A new study praising eggs
A fall in household incomes
A drop in the price of cereal
review.why: Losing hens cuts what farms can offer at every price; the other choices affect demand or lower it.

review.q: Why do economists say pollution is a market failure rather than simply a bad thing?
choices: Because polluters always break the law
Because the price of the product leaves out the cost imposed on outsiders
Because pollution raises GDP
Because pollution is a public good
review.why: An externality means the market price is wrong, so buyers get more of the product than its true cost justifies.

review.q: Which agency raised interest rates sharply between 2022 and 2023 to fight inflation?
choices: Congress through fiscal policy
The Illinois General Assembly
The Treasury Department
The Federal Reserve through monetary policy
review.why: Setting interest rates is the Fed's job; Congress controls taxes and spending instead.

review.q: In April 2020 the unemployment rate was about fifteen percent. What made that spike different from 1982 or 2009?
choices: It lasted for many years
It was caused by inflation
It was caused by a sudden shutdown and fell within months
It affected only farm workers
review.why: The pandemic shutdown was sharp but brief; the 1982 and 2009 recessions took years to recover from.

review.q: The federal government put a tariff on imported steel in 2018. Which effect did economists expect and observe?
choices: Steel prices fell for American carmakers
Protected steel jobs, higher costs for steel users and retaliation against farm exports
Soybean exports to China increased
The national debt was paid down
review.why: A tariff helps the protected industry while raising costs for buyers and inviting retaliation, which hit Illinois soybean farmers.

review.q: Which statement about the national debt is supported by the chapter?
choices: It has grown under both parties because raising taxes and cutting spending are both unpopular
It was eliminated in 2020
It is owed only to foreign countries
It is the same as the yearly deficit
review.why: Shrinking the debt requires unpopular choices, so it has kept growing regardless of which party held power.

review.q: Two eighteen-year-olds each save one thousand dollars. One invests it in a diversified index fund and leaves it forty years; the other keeps it in cash. What best explains the difference at age fifty-eight?
choices: The FAFSA
A price ceiling
Insurance premiums
Compound growth over a long time
review.why: At about seven percent a year, compounding turns one thousand dollars into roughly fifteen thousand over forty years, while cash loses value to inflation.
